d1-001.a: Agility refers to the ability to rapidly innovate and deliver resources to developers quickly, rather than eliminating data center operational costs.
d1-001.c: Deploying globally in minutes refers to the ability to expand applications to multiple AWS Regions worldwide with minimal latency, not the reduction of physical infrastructure costs.
d1-001.d: Elasticity refers to the ability to automatically scale computing resources up or down based on current demand, rather than the elimination of data center maintenance expenses.

d1-002.a: High availability focuses on keeping systems operational and accessible with minimal downtime, not on dynamically adjusting resources to match capacity needs.
d1-002.b: Economies of scale refers to lower variable costs resulting from aggregate usage across many customers, rather than the ability to scale infrastructure based on demand.
d1-002.d: Agility describes the speed and flexibility of provisioning resources quickly to innovate faster, rather than eliminating the need to predict capacity.

d1-003.a: IaaS provides raw infrastructure building blocks like virtual machines, storage, and networking, leaving the customer responsible for installing and managing the operating system and applications. It does not deliver a finished, fully managed application.
d1-003.b: PaaS provides a platform for developers to deploy and run code without managing underlying servers, but customers are still responsible for developing and maintaining the application itself. It does not provide a completed, ready-to-use end-user product.
d1-003.d: FaaS allows developers to run modular pieces of code in response to events without managing servers, rather than offering a full application interface. Users must write and maintain their own application logic rather than consuming a pre-built software service.

d1-004.a: A private cloud model hosts all infrastructure on-premises or exclusively for a single organization, without integrating public cloud resources.
d1-004.b: A community cloud is shared by multiple organizations with common concerns, rather than a single organization combining its local data center with AWS.
d1-004.d: A public cloud deployment runs all infrastructure and applications entirely within the cloud provider's environment, with no on-premises data center integration.

d1-005.a: The Security pillar focuses on protecting data, systems, and assets through confidentiality, integrity, and risk management strategies rather than managing operational processes.
d1-005.b: The Reliability pillar focuses on ensuring a workload performs its intended function correctly and consistently, including recovering from operational or infrastructure disruptions.
d1-005.d: The Performance Efficiency pillar focuses on using computing resources efficiently to meet system requirements and maintaining that efficiency as demand changes and technology evolves.

d1-006.b: AWS CloudFormation is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) service used to model and provision AWS resources using templates, rather than managing or visualizing cloud migrations.
d1-006.c: AWS Trusted Advisor focuses on optimizing your AWS environment for cost, security, performance, and fault tolerance, not on defining or tracking migration strategies.
d1-006.d: AWS Config is used to assess, audit, and evaluate the configurations of your AWS resources for compliance, rather than guiding application migrations to the cloud.

d1-007.b: While scalability is a key cloud concept, it is a design principle evaluated within pillars like Reliability and Performance Efficiency, not a standalone pillar itself.
d1-007.c: Elasticity is an architectural best practice used to adapt to changing demand, but it is considered a technique within the framework rather than one of the six main pillars.
d1-007.e: The framework focuses on financial management through the Cost Optimization pillar, whereas Affordability is not a formal AWS Well-Architected pillar name.

d1-008.a: Replatforming involves making minor optimizations or infrastructure tweaks to the application to take advantage of cloud capabilities without altering its core architecture.
d1-008.b: Refactoring requires redesigning and rewriting the application code to make it fully cloud-native and take full advantage of cloud features.
d1-008.d: Repurchasing involves replacing the existing application entirely by switching to a different product or a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform.

d1-009.a: 'Go global in minutes' refers to deploying applications in multiple AWS Regions worldwide quickly to reduce latency for users, rather than converting capital expenses to variable costs.
d1-009.b: 'Stop guessing capacity' focuses on dynamically adjusting resources to avoid over- or under-provisioning, rather than addressing upfront capital investments.
d1-009.d: 'Increase speed and agility' relates to reducing the time required to provision IT resources to accelerate innovation, not reducing initial infrastructure expenditures.

d1-010.a: Elasticity refers to the ability to dynamically scale resources up or down based on demand, which helps optimize usage rather than reducing the base unit costs through aggregated purchasing power.
d1-010.c: High availability ensures that systems remain operational and accessible with minimal downtime, focusing on infrastructure reliability rather than cost reduction.
d1-010.d: Fault tolerance is a system's capability to continue operating seamlessly when a component fails, which is a resiliency feature rather than a financial advantage.

d1-011.a: Performance Efficiency focuses on using computing resources efficiently to meet system requirements and maintaining that efficiency as demand changes, rather than ensuring consistent functional execution.
d1-011.b: The Security pillar focuses on protecting data, systems, and assets through risk assessment and mitigation strategies, rather than ensuring operational consistency.
d1-011.d: Cost Optimization focuses on running systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point, rather than ensuring a workload performs its intended function correctly.

d1-012.a: Rehost (lift-and-shift) involves moving an application to the cloud without making any changes to its core architecture, which does not apply when breaking a monolith into microservices.
d1-012.b: Replatform involves making minor optimizations to the environment or infrastructure without modifying the application's underlying code or architecture.
d1-012.d: Retire involves turning off or decommissioning applications that are no longer needed, rather than modernizing them.

d1-013.a: Hardware and software failures are inevitable in any environment, so assuming components will never fail is unrealistic. Instead, systems should be designed to handle and recover from failures automatically when they occur.
d1-013.c: Using expensive services does not guarantee immunity from failures. Reliability in the cloud is achieved through architectural strategies like redundancy and fault tolerance rather than higher spending on single components.
d1-013.d: Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, customers are responsible for designing resilient applications that handle failover automatically, rather than relying on manual intervention from AWS support.

d1-014.a: This refers to global reach, not agility.
d1-014.d: This refers to high availability and reliability.

d1-015.a: Trusted Advisor provides real-time guidance on best practices, but it doesn't use a questionnaire format to evaluate against the framework.
d1-015.c: CloudTrail tracks user activity and API usage, it does not evaluate architecture.
d1-015.d: Config is used to assess, audit, and evaluate the configurations of your AWS resources, not architecture best practices.

d1-016.a: Rehosting or 'lift and shift' involves moving an application to AWS without making any changes.
d1-016.c: Retaining involves keeping the application in its current environment without migrating it.
d1-016.d: Replatforming involves making minor optimizations to the application while migrating it to the cloud.

d1-017.a: This pillar focuses on running and monitoring systems to deliver business value.
d1-017.b: This pillar focuses on avoiding unnecessary costs.
d1-017.d: This pillar focuses on ensuring a workload performs its intended function correctly and consistently.

d1-018.a: Latency for global users is reduced by using Edge Locations or multiple AWS Regions, not just Availability Zones within one Region.
d1-018.b: Deploying across multiple Availability Zones generally increases costs due to additional resources.
d1-018.d: Building highly available applications across multiple Availability Zones adds complexity rather than simplifying development.

d1-019.b: The People perspective focuses on organizational structure and culture, not business alignment.
d1-019.c: The Governance perspective focuses on measuring cloud investments and risk management.
d1-019.d: The Platform perspective focuses on IT infrastructure and architecture.

d1-020.b: Cloud computing typically uses pay-as-you-go pricing without requiring long-term contracts.
d1-020.d: Cloud computing provides elastic, scalable capacity rather than fixed capacity.
d1-020.e: Cloud computing abstracts physical hardware management, which is handled by the cloud provider.

d1-021.a: Rehost (lift and shift) involves migrating an application exactly as-is without any optimizations.
d1-021.c: Refactor involves significantly changing the application's architecture (e.g., making it cloud-native).
d1-021.d: Relocate involves moving infrastructure (like VMware) to the cloud without changing the underlying software.

d1-022.a: Cost Optimization focuses on avoiding unnecessary expenses, not compute efficiency.
d1-022.b: Reliability focuses on preventing and recovering from failures.
d1-022.c: Operational Excellence focuses on running and monitoring systems to deliver business value.

d1-023.a: Managed services typically abstract the underlying OS, so you do not have complete control over it.
d1-023.c: Managed services may have higher upfront costs than self-hosted open-source software, though they save on operational costs.
d1-023.d: You are still responsible for configuring security settings like access controls and network rules under the shared responsibility model.

d1-024.b: AWS CloudFormation is used to provision resources using Infrastructure as Code (IaC).
d1-024.c: Amazon Inspector is an automated security assessment service.
d1-024.d: AWS CodeDeploy automates application deployments to compute services.

d1-025.a: While automation is a best practice, it is typically part of Operational Excellence and doesn't refer to reversibility.
d1-025.c: Anticipating failure is a design principle for Reliability.
d1-025.d: Using serverless architectures is a design principle for Performance Efficiency, not related to reversible increments.

d1-026.b: The cloud replaces upfront capital expenses (CapEx) with pay-as-you-go variable expenses (OpEx), not the other way around.
d1-026.c: Customers pay based on actual usage, not a fixed monthly fee.
d1-026.d: Hardware maintenance costs are borne by the cloud provider, not billed annually to the customer.

d1-027.a: Agility refers to the speed of provisioning resources and innovating.
d1-027.c: Elasticity is the ability to automatically scale resources in or out to meet demand.
d1-027.d: Economy of scale refers to lower costs achieved through massive cloud provider infrastructure.

d1-028.a: AWS Trusted Advisor provides real-time checks on cost, performance, and security, but not a guided framework evaluation.
d1-028.c: AWS Config tracks and evaluates resource configuration changes over time.
d1-028.d: Amazon Inspector evaluates applications for security vulnerabilities.

d1-029.a: High Availability refers to systems being accessible with minimal downtime.
d1-029.b: Fault Tolerance refers to a system's ability to remain operational even if some components fail.
d1-029.d: Disaster Recovery focuses on recovering data and infrastructure after a major disruption.

d1-030.a: The Business Perspective helps ensure that IT aligns with business needs and that IT investments link to key business results.
d1-030.c: The Operations Perspective focuses on operating and recovering IT workloads to meet the requirements of your business stakeholders.
d1-030.d: The Security Perspective helps structure the selection and implementation of controls.

d1-031.a: Security assessments are still necessary and are unrelated to capacity guessing.
d1-031.c: Automating AWS accounts is unrelated to capacity limits.
d1-031.d: Multi-AZ deployments are a high availability best practice, unrelated to capacity guessing.

d1-032.a: Hybrid Cloud involves keeping some resources on-premises while moving others to the cloud.
d1-032.c: Multi-Cloud involves using multiple different public cloud providers (e.g., AWS and Azure).
d1-032.d: On-premises deployment is the opposite of migrating to the cloud.

d1-033.a: Massive economies of scale refers to AWS's ability to lower costs due to its large infrastructure, not innovation speed.
d1-033.c: Global footprint refers to AWS having data centers worldwide.
d1-033.d: Trading CapEx for OpEx is a financial benefit, not a direct enabler of rapid innovation.

d1-034.a: Replatforming (lift, tinker, and shift) involves making minor optimizations to the application.
d1-034.c: Refactoring involves rewriting or reimagining the application architecture using cloud-native features.
d1-034.d: Repurchasing involves abandoning the current application and moving to a SaaS product.

d1-035.a: Operational Excellence focuses on running and monitoring systems to deliver business value.
d1-035.b: Security focuses on protecting information, systems, and assets.
d1-035.d: Performance Efficiency focuses on using IT and compute resources efficiently to meet system requirements.

d1-036.a: Rehosting is simply moving the application as-is without changing its architecture.
d1-036.b: Replatforming involves minor optimizations, not a complete architectural overhaul like monolithic to microservices.
d1-036.d: Retaining involves keeping the application in its current environment and doing nothing.

d1-037.b: AWS does not manage all security aspects; customers are responsible for securing their data, OS, and applications.
d1-037.c: AWS is responsible for the physical security of its data centers.
d1-037.d: The customer is solely responsible for configuring IAM policies (Security IN the cloud).

d1-038.a: AWS offers pay-as-you-go pricing; long-term contracts are optional (e.g., Reserved Instances).
d1-038.c: AWS uses proprietary and open-source software, but this is not the cause of their economies of scale.
d1-038.d: AWS has many global data centers across different Regions and Availability Zones, not just one.

d1-039.a: Running instances in multiple Regions typically increases costs due to using more resources.
d1-039.c: AWS does not automatically translate applications; this requires specific services or development.
d1-039.d: While it improves availability, AWS does not guarantee 100% uptime with zero downtime.

d1-040.b: Implementing a strong identity foundation is a design principle for the Security pillar.
d1-040.c: Enabling traceability is a design principle for the Security pillar.
d1-040.d: Performing operations as code is a design principle for the Operational Excellence pillar.

d2-001.a: Managing IAM users and their permissions is the customer's responsibility (Security IN the Cloud).
d2-001.b: Patching the guest OS on EC2 is the customer's responsibility.
d2-001.d: Encrypting application data is the customer's responsibility.

d2-002.a: AWS Shield provides Managed DDoS protection.
d2-002.c: AWS WAF is a web application firewall to protect against common web exploits.
d2-002.d: Amazon Macie uses machine learning to discover and protect sensitive data in AWS.

d2-003.a: IAM Groups are collections of users, not mechanisms for providing temporary access.
d2-003.b: IAM Policies define permissions, but do not provide the temporary credentials themselves.
d2-003.d: IAM Access Analyzer helps identify unintended access to your resources and data.

d2-004.a: CloudTrail records API calls and user activity, but GuardDuty analyzes them for threats.
d2-004.c: AWS Config tracks configuration changes to AWS resources, not malicious network activity.
d2-004.d: AWS Trusted Advisor provides best practices across cost, performance, and security, but does not actively detect threats.

d2-005.a: The root user should only be used for specific tasks that require it, not daily administration.
d2-005.b: Root credentials should never be shared.
d2-005.d: It is highly recommended NOT to create access keys for the root user due to security risks.

d2-006.a: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks, mostly at Layers 3 and 4.
d2-006.b: Security Groups are stateful instance-level firewalls, not Layer 7 application firewalls.
d2-006.d: Network ACLs are stateless subnet-level firewalls, operating below Layer 7.

d2-007.b: AWS is responsible for maintaining the physical networking equipment.
d2-007.d: AWS is responsible for decommissioning hardware securely.
d2-007.e: AWS is responsible for patching the underlying hypervisor (host OS).

d2-008.a: AWS WAF protects against common web exploits like SQL injection and XSS at Layer 7.
d2-008.c: Amazon GuardDuty provides intelligent threat detection, not direct DDoS protection.
d2-008.d: AWS Firewall Manager simplifies management of WAF, Shield, and security groups across accounts.

d2-009.a: An IAM User represents a specific person or service, not a mechanism to delegate temporary access.
d2-009.b: An IAM Group is a collection of IAM users used to manage permissions for multiple users at once.
d2-009.c: An IAM Policy is a document defining permissions, not an entity that assumes those permissions.

d2-010.a: AWS Artifact provides access to AWS compliance reports, not a centralized view of your own compliance status.
d2-010.c: AWS CloudTrail logs API activity but does not provide a centralized compliance dashboard.
d2-010.d: Amazon Inspector assesses individual applications for vulnerabilities, not overall account compliance.

d2-011.a: AWS Security Hub provides a centralized view of security alerts and compliance status across accounts.
d2-011.c: AWS Config tracks configuration changes to resources against desired configurations.
d2-011.d: AWS Audit Manager helps continuously audit your AWS usage to simplify risk and compliance assessment.

d2-012.a: IAM Groups are collections of users, not the actual JSON documents that define permissions.
d2-012.b: IAM Roles are entities that assume permissions, but they use policies to define those permissions.
d2-012.d: IAM Identity Center manages single sign-on access, it does not define fine-grained JSON controls natively.

d2-013.a: Amazon CloudWatch monitors performance metrics and application logs, not account-level API calls.
d2-013.c: AWS Config tracks changes to resource configurations, not the API calls themselves.
d2-013.d: AWS X-Ray traces user requests traveling through your application for debugging, not auditing API calls.

d2-014.a: CloudTrail records who made an API call, but does not actively evaluate resource configurations against rules.
d2-014.b: Trusted Advisor provides high-level guidance on best practices, but does not continuously track specific resource configurations.
d2-014.d: Systems Manager is used to view and control infrastructure, not for compliance monitoring of resource configurations.

d2-015.a: Granting administrative access to everyone violates least privilege and creates massive security risks.
d2-015.c: Permissions should be based on the specific tasks a user needs to perform, not just their seniority.
d2-015.d: The root account already has all permissions; least privilege applies to IAM users and roles.

d2-016.a: Amazon GuardDuty analyzes network and API events for malicious activity, not S3 data content.
d2-016.c: Amazon Inspector analyzes applications and EC2 instances for vulnerabilities, not data classification.
d2-016.d: AWS Secrets Manager stores and manages credentials, it does not discover PII in data stores.

d2-017.a: AWS KMS manages encryption keys, not database credentials.
d2-017.b: Parameter Store can store secrets, but does not natively provide built-in automatic credential rotation for databases like Secrets Manager.
d2-017.d: AWS Certificate Manager provisions and manages SSL/TLS certificates, not database credentials.

d2-018.a: Network ACLs act as firewalls at the subnet level, not the instance level.
d2-018.c: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that operates at Layer 7, typically attached to ALBs or API Gateways, not instances.
d2-018.d: AWS Shield provides DDoS protection, not instance-level firewall rules.

d2-019.a: AWS IAM manages users and roles within a single account, not centralized single sign-on across multiple accounts.
d2-019.c: Amazon Cognito manages identity for web and mobile applications (customer identities), not workforce SSO.
d2-019.d: AWS Directory Service provides managed Active Directory, but Identity Center is specifically for managing SSO access.

d2-020.a: MFA has nothing to do with encrypting data at rest.
d2-020.c: MFA is for authentication, not for automating backups.
d2-020.d: MFA is for authentication, not for enabling replication features.

d2-021.a: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service for malicious activity, not a vulnerability assessment tool.
d2-021.c: AWS Artifact provides access to AWS compliance reports and agreements.
d2-021.d: AWS Security Hub aggregates alerts and compliance status, but relies on tools like Inspector for actual vulnerability scanning.

d2-022.a: Network ACLs are stateless, meaning they do NOT automatically allow return traffic; you must explicitly allow it.
d2-022.b: Network ACLs operate at the subnet level. Security Groups operate at the instance level.
d2-022.d: Network ACLs support both allow and deny rules.

d2-023.a: AWS Shield provides managed DDoS protection, it does not centrally manage firewall rules.
d2-023.c: Amazon GuardDuty detects threats; it is not a firewall management service.
d2-023.d: AWS CloudTrail logs API calls for auditing purposes.

d2-024.a: AWS Secrets Manager is for database credentials and API keys, not SSL/TLS certificates.
d2-024.c: AWS KMS is for data encryption keys, not SSL/TLS certificates.
d2-024.d: AWS CloudHSM provides hardware security modules for key storage, but does not directly provision SSL/TLS certificates.

d2-025.a: Least privilege refers to giving minimal permissions, not the act of giving each person their own account.
d2-025.b: Defense in depth refers to using multiple layers of security controls.
d2-025.d: Encryption at rest protects data stored on disks, not user accountability.

d2-026.a: S3 Versioning keeps multiple variants of an object, but does not prevent deletion of those versions.
d2-026.c: S3 Lifecycle policies automatically move or delete objects after a certain time, rather than preventing deletion.
d2-026.d: S3 Cross-Region Replication copies objects to another region, but does not prevent deletion.

d2-027.a: AWS KMS uses multi-tenant HSMs. CloudHSM provides dedicated single-tenant hardware.
d2-027.c: AWS Secrets Manager manages credentials and API keys, not hardware modules.

d2-028.a: SCPs cannot grant permissions; they only set boundaries (maximum permissions). IAM policies are needed to grant access.
d2-028.c: SCPs do not enforce encryption; they only restrict actions.
d2-028.d: SCPs are for access control, not for billing or reporting.

d2-029.b: Client-Side Encryption requires you to encrypt data before sending it to S3, but it's not managed via IAM policies.
d2-029.d: Security Groups control network access to instances, they do not encrypt data.
d2-029.e: Network ACLs control network access to subnets, they do not encrypt data.

d2-030.a: AWS IAM manages permissions for AWS resources, not identities for your customer-facing applications.
d2-030.b: IAM Identity Center manages workforce single sign-on, not customer identities.
d2-030.d: AWS Directory Service provides managed Active Directory for workforce users.

d2-031.b: Configuring IAM is the customer's responsibility (Security IN the cloud).
d2-031.c: Patching the guest OS on EC2 is the customer's responsibility.
d2-031.d: Encrypting customer data at rest is the customer's responsibility.

d2-032.a: AWS Shield provides DDoS protection, not protection against application-layer exploits like SQL injection.
d2-032.c: Amazon GuardDuty detects threats by analyzing logs, but it does not act as a firewall to protect web apps.
d2-032.d: Amazon Inspector assesses EC2 instances and containers for vulnerabilities, but does not block web exploits.

d2-033.b: AWS Audit Manager continuously audits your AWS usage to assess risk, but Artifact provides the actual compliance reports.
d2-033.c: AWS CloudTrail logs API activity, it does not provide compliance reports.
d2-033.d: AWS Config tracks configuration changes, not compliance reports like SOC or PCI.

d2-034.a: Amazon Inspector evaluates applications for vulnerabilities, not continuous monitoring for malicious activity.
d2-034.c: AWS CloudTrail logs API activity, but GuardDuty actively analyzes those logs for threats.
d2-034.d: Amazon Macie discovers and protects sensitive data, it does not monitor for malicious account activity.

d2-035.a: Managing user identities is done by AWS IAM or Amazon Cognito, not KMS.
d2-035.c: Storing MFA tokens is done by IAM or an authenticator app, not KMS.
d2-035.d: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions SSL/TLS certificates, not KMS.

d2-036.b: Amazon Inspector assesses vulnerabilities on EC2 and ECR, not sensitive data discovery.
d2-036.d: Amazon GuardDuty detects malicious activity and threats, not sensitive data classification.

d2-037.a: Granting full access violates the principle of least privilege and introduces severe security risks.
d2-037.c: Using inline policies for everyone makes management difficult; managed policies are generally preferred.
d2-037.d: Root user credentials should never be shared.

d2-038.a: AWS WAF protects against web exploits like SQL injection, while Shield protects against DDoS attacks.
d2-038.c: Amazon Inspector assesses vulnerabilities, it does not provide DDoS protection.
d2-038.d: AWS Secrets Manager manages credentials and API keys.

d2-039.a: While Parameter Store can store secrets, Secrets Manager includes built-in automated credential rotation.
d2-039.c: AWS KMS manages encryption keys, not the actual database credentials.
d2-039.d: AWS IAM manages permissions and users, not database credentials.

d2-040.a: AWS IAM manages permissions within a single account, not across multiple accounts natively without Organizations.
d2-040.c: AWS Security Hub aggregates security alerts, it does not enforce policies.
d2-040.d: AWS Trusted Advisor provides best practice recommendations, it does not enforce policies.

d2-041.a: AWS CloudTrail records API calls but does not provide a comprehensive dashboard of security alerts.
d2-041.c: Amazon Inspector only provides vulnerability assessments for specific resources, not a comprehensive security view.
d2-041.d: Amazon CloudWatch monitors performance metrics and logs.

d2-042.a: An IAM User uniquely identifies a human user or service account, not a Role.
d2-042.b: AWS Secrets Manager securely stores passwords, not IAM Roles.
d2-042.d: VPC Subnets and Security Groups define network boundaries, not IAM Roles.

d2-043.a: AWS is responsible for patching the underlying OS for managed services like Amazon RDS.
d2-043.b: AWS is responsible for managing the physical hardware.
d2-043.d: AWS is responsible for installing the database software for Amazon RDS.

d2-044.c: Amazon GuardDuty detects malicious activity and threats, not software vulnerabilities.
d2-044.d: AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes.

d2-045.a: AWS Config tracks configuration changes, not the history of all API calls.
d2-045.b: Amazon CloudWatch monitors performance metrics, not the audit trail of API calls.
d2-045.d: AWS Artifact provides compliance reports and agreements.

d3-001.a: AWS Lambda runs code without provisioning or managing servers (serverless).
d3-001.c: Amazon S3 provides object storage, not compute capacity.
d3-001.d: Amazon RDS provides managed relational databases, not general-purpose virtual servers.

d3-002.a: Amazon EC2 requires you to provision and manage virtual servers.
d3-002.b: Amazon ECS manages containers, but you still manage the underlying EC2 servers (unless using Fargate).
d3-002.d: AWS Elastic Beanstalk provisions and manages underlying resources like EC2 for you, but they still exist as servers you can access.

d3-003.a: S3 Standard is for frequently accessed data, not rarely accessed data.
d3-003.b: S3 Standard-IA is for rarely accessed data but is more expensive than Glacier Instant Retrieval for very infrequent access.
d3-003.d: S3 Glacier Deep Archive has retrieval times of hours, not milliseconds.

d3-004.a: Amazon DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL (non-relational) database, not a relational database.
d3-004.b: Amazon Redshift is a data warehousing service, not a standard relational database for OLTP workloads.
d3-004.d: Amazon ElastiCache provides managed in-memory data stores (Redis and Memcached), not relational databases.

d3-005.a: Amazon Route 53 is a highly available Domain Name System (DNS) web service, not a CDN.
d3-005.c: AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated private network connection from on-premises to AWS, not a CDN.
d3-005.d: Amazon VPC allows you to provision a logically isolated section of the AWS Cloud, not deliver content globally.

d3-006.a: Amazon RDS is a relational database service, not a NoSQL database.
d3-006.b: Amazon Aurora is a MySQL and PostgreSQL-compatible relational database, not NoSQL.
d3-006.d: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse service used for analytical queries (OLAP).

d3-007.a: Edge locations are endpoints for AWS CloudFront (CDN) to cache content, not the primary compute infrastructure of a Region.
d3-007.c: An Availability Zone consists of one or more discrete data centers, so a data center is just a component of an AZ.
d3-007.d: Local Zones place compute and storage resources closer to large populations, industry, and IT centers, but are extensions of a Region, not its core components.

d3-008.a: AWS CodeDeploy automates application deployments, not infrastructure provisioning via templates.
d3-008.c: AWS Systems Manager gives you visibility and control of your infrastructure, but does not primarily use templates for initial provisioning.
d3-008.d: AWS OpsWorks is a configuration management service that provides managed instances of Chef and Puppet, not standard Infrastructure as Code templates.

d3-009.a: AWS CloudTrail logs API calls for auditing, it does not provide performance monitoring or custom alarms.
d3-009.c: AWS Config tracks configuration changes to your resources, it does not monitor performance metrics.
d3-009.d: AWS X-Ray analyzes and debugs distributed applications (like microservices), it is not a general monitoring dashboard.

d3-010.a: Amazon CloudFront is a Content Delivery Network (CDN), not a DNS service.
d3-010.c: Elastic Load Balancing automatically distributes incoming application traffic, it does not resolve domain names.
d3-010.d: Amazon API Gateway allows developers to create, publish, and secure APIs, not manage DNS.

d3-011.a: With Amazon EC2, you must provision and manage the underlying virtual servers yourself.
d3-011.b: AWS Lambda runs code (functions) without managing servers, but it is not a service specifically for running Docker containers.
d3-011.d: Amazon Lightsail provides easy-to-use virtual private servers, requiring you to manage the server instance.

d3-012.a: Amazon S3 provides object-level storage, not block-level storage.
d3-012.b: Amazon EFS provides file-level storage (file systems) for use with EC2 instances.
d3-012.d: AWS Storage Gateway connects on-premises software appliances with cloud-based storage, it is not an EC2 block storage volume.

d3-013.a: Amazon EBS provides block storage volumes that are typically attached to a single EC2 instance, not shared across many.
d3-013.b: Amazon S3 is object storage accessed via API over the internet, not a traditional file system.
d3-013.d: AWS Storage Gateway bridges on-premises environments with AWS cloud storage.

d3-014.a: Amazon Route 53 routes users to internet applications via DNS, but ELB handles the distribution of traffic within a VPC.
d3-014.b: Amazon CloudFront delivers content via edge locations; it is not a load balancer for EC2 targets.

td-013.a: Amazon Aurora is a fully-managed service that automates tasks like hardware provisioning, database setup, patching, and backups. You do not manage the guest operating system.
td-013.b: Amazon EC2 gives you control over the instance, allowing you to install any database, manage the guest operating system, apply updates and security patches yourself.
td-013.c: Amazon DocumentDB is a fully-managed document database service. You don't need to handle the guest operating system since it is managed by AWS.
td-013.d: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully-managed NoSQL database service. The underlying operating system is managed by AWS, not the customer.

td-014.a: Enterprise Support provides a 4-hour response time when your production system is impaired, not 2 hours.
td-014.b: Enterprise Support provides a 15-minute response time when your business-critical system goes down, the fastest response time available.
td-014.c: Enterprise Support provides a 24-hour response time for general guidance, not 48 hours.
td-014.d: Enterprise Support provides a 1-hour response time when your production system goes down.
td-014.e: Enterprise Support provides a 24-hour response time for general guidance, not 12 hours.

td-015.a: This is incorrect because the requirement can be fulfilled by a Network Load Balancer, which operates at Layer 4 for TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic.
td-015.b: Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and is not designed for TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic load balancing.
td-015.c: Gateway Load Balancer passes all Layer 3 traffic through third-party virtual appliances. It is not primarily designed for what a Network Load Balancer does.
td-015.d: Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and is best suited for TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic where extreme performance is required. It handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latencies.

td-016.a: AWS GovCloud is an isolated AWS Region for U.S. government agencies to meet regulatory requirements. It is not a compliance document repository.
td-016.b: AWS Audit Manager helps automate evidence collection for audits but does not directly provide compliance reports like SOC 1 or SOC 2. It prepares for audits, not reports.
td-016.c: AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS security and compliance reports including SOC reports, PCI reports, and ISO certifications. It is the central resource for compliance documents.
td-016.d: AWS Certificate Manager provisions, manages, and deploys SSL/TLS certificates. It does not store compliance certifications or reports.

td-017.a: AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to compliance reports including SOC, PCI, and ISO certifications that validate AWS security controls. All AWS accounts have access.
td-017.b: AWS Trusted Advisor provides real-time guidance following AWS best practices for cost, performance, security, and fault tolerance. It doesn't store compliance documents.
td-017.c: AWS Certificate Manager manages SSL/TLS certificates, not compliance-related documents or audit reports.
td-017.d: AWS Security Token Service generates temporary credentials for accessing AWS resources. It is not designed for retrieving compliance reports.

td-018.a: Configuration Management is a shared control. AWS maintains its infrastructure configuration, while customers configure their own guest operating systems, databases, and applications.
td-018.b: Patching the host operating system is AWS's responsibility. The customer patches the guest OS and applications, not the host OS.
td-018.c: Service and Communications Protection or Zone Security is a Customer Specific control — solely the customer's responsibility, such as routing or zoning data within specific security environments.
td-018.d: Awareness & Training is a shared control. AWS trains its own employees, but customers must train their own employees.

td-019.a: Agile methodologies promote iterative development, frequent customer feedback, and continuous improvement, enabling the company to respond quickly to customer needs and deliver value continuously.
td-019.b: Transitioning legacy infrastructure focuses on technical infrastructure modernization, not directly on organizational transformation or customer-centric team collaboration.
td-019.c: A data and analytics platform generates insights but does not directly address optimizing operations, delivery processes, or promoting team collaboration for customer focus.
td-019.d: Restructuring teams to prioritize product-focused and value stream-oriented approaches fosters cross-functional collaboration and ensures alignment with strategic objectives focused on customer value.
td-019.e: Introducing new products and revenue models focuses on product transformation and innovation, not directly on organizational transformation or team collaboration.

td-020.a: Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and targets EC2 instances, containers, and IP addresses. It does not support Lambda functions as targets.
td-020.b: Neither Gateway Load Balancer nor Network Load Balancer supports Lambda functions as targets. Only Application Load Balancer does.
td-020.c: Application Load Balancer can register Lambda functions as targets. When a request is forwarded to a Lambda target group, it invokes the function and passes the request content in JSON format.
td-020.d: Gateway Load Balancer routes Layer 3 traffic through third-party virtual appliances. It does not support Lambda functions as targets.

td-021.a: Technical Account Management is part of AWS Enterprise Support. A TAM provides advocacy and guidance but is not a consulting firm that designs and builds applications.
td-021.b: AWS Marketplace is a channel for ISVs and Consulting Partners to sell software solutions. It does not provide consulting services to design and build applications.
td-021.c: APN Technology Partners provide software solutions hosted on or integrated with AWS, such as ISVs and SaaS vendors. They don't help design and architect workloads.
td-021.d: APN Consulting Partners are professional services firms that help customers design, architect, migrate, or build new applications on AWS, including SIs, Strategic Consultancies, and MSPs.

td-022.a: AWS Security Token Service is considered a global service, available in all regions without needing region-specific configuration.
td-022.b: Amazon EC2 is a zonal service because instances are tied to the specific Availability Zone where they were launched.
td-022.c: Amazon EFS is a regional service that stores data within and across multiple Availability Zones for high availability and durability.
td-022.d: AWS Billing Conductor is a global billing management service that operates across all AWS Regions and does not require region selection.
td-022.e: AWS Batch is a regional service that simplifies running batch jobs across multiple Availability Zones within a region.

td-023.a: This is incorrect because patching the host operating system is AWS's responsibility. It falls under AWS's side of the shared responsibility model.
td-023.b: AWS manages the host operating system (hypervisor), the virtualization layer, and the physical security of the facilities. The customer manages the guest operating system.
td-023.c: Patching the host operating system is solely AWS's responsibility, not a shared task. The customer handles the guest OS, and AWS handles the host OS.
td-023.d: The customer is responsible for patching the guest operating system, not the host OS. The host OS (hypervisor) is managed by AWS.

td-024.a: CloudFront primarily caches and delivers static content from edge locations. For real-time gaming, server interactions require servers physically closer to players, not just a CDN.
td-024.b: Autoscaling can handle varying player loads but won't solve latency issues caused by physical distance between servers in Virginia and players in Europe/Asia.
td-024.c: AWS Direct Connect optimizes network routing and can reduce latency somewhat, but it may not be sufficient for latency-sensitive gaming applications across continents.
td-024.d: Deploying game servers in Europe and Asia minimizes the physical distance data needs to travel, resulting in significantly faster response times and a smoother gaming experience.

td-025.a: A Dedicated Host is a physical server fully dedicated to your use, allowing you to use existing per-socket, per-core, or per-VM software licenses (BYOL) and address compliance requirements.
td-025.b: Reserved Instances provide discounted pricing but do not allow you to use your own server-bound software licenses.
td-025.c: Dedicated Instances run on dedicated hardware but lack the visibility and control over instance placement on a specific physical server that Dedicated Hosts provide for licensing compliance.
td-025.d: On-Demand Instances provide flexible pay-as-you-go pricing but do not allow you to use your existing server-bound software licenses.

td-026.a: Concierge Support is a team of billing and account experts that assist with billing inquiries under Enterprise Support. They don't provide software solutions.
td-026.b: Technical Account Management is part of Enterprise Support providing advocacy and guidance. It is not a category of partners providing software solutions.
td-026.c: APN Technology Partners provide software solutions hosted on or integrated with the AWS platform, including ISVs, SaaS, PaaS, developer tools, management, and security vendors.
td-026.d: APN Consulting Partners help customers design, architect, migrate, or build applications on AWS. They don't provide software solutions hosted on the platform.

td-027.a: Amazon VPC lets you provision a logically isolated section of the AWS Cloud with complete control over IP address ranges, subnets, route tables, and network gateways.
td-027.b: An Internet gateway enables communication between your VPC and the public internet. It does not isolate a virtual network space for launching resources.
td-027.c: AWS Elastic Beanstalk is a platform for deploying web applications that handles infrastructure provisioning. It does not provision an isolated network section.
td-027.d: Amazon EC2 is a compute service for hosting applications on virtual servers. It does not provision an isolated virtual network.

td-028.a: The 15-minute response time for a business-critical system down is only available with Enterprise Support, not Business Support+.
td-028.b: Business Support+ provides a 4-hour response time when your production system is impaired, not 1 hour.
td-028.c: Business Support+ guarantees a response time of less than 1 hour when a production system is down. This is the correct response time for this support tier.
td-028.d: The 15-minute response time for production system down is not available with Business Support+. Business Support+ offers 1-hour response for production system down.

td-029.a: A security group acts as a virtual firewall at the instance level, controlling inbound and outbound traffic. You can assign up to five security groups to each instance.
td-029.b: Network ACLs protect subnets by controlling inbound and outbound traffic at the subnet level, not at the individual instance level.
td-029.c: An Elastic Network Interface is a logical networking component representing a virtual network card. It does not serve as a firewall.
td-029.d: VPC is a logically isolated section of the AWS Cloud for launching resources. It is the network itself, not a firewall for individual instances.

td-030.a: AWS does not simply wipe and dispose of devices. They follow strict decommissioning procedures as described in NIST 800-88 compliance guidelines.
td-030.b: AWS does not send drives back to manufacturers. Media that stored customer data is not removed from AWS control until securely decommissioned.
td-030.c: AWS classifies media storage devices as Critical and follows a strict decommissioning process using techniques detailed in NIST 800-88. Media is not removed from AWS control until securely decommissioned.
td-030.d: AWS does not archive devices after their lifespan ends. Devices are securely decommissioned following strict compliance procedures.

oa-001.a: Amazon Connect is an omnichannel cloud contact center for customer service. It does not provide a network connection between on-premises and AWS.
oa-001.b: Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted network path between your on-premises network and AWS Cloud network using your existing internet connection.
oa-001.c: CloudFront is a CDN that speeds up distribution of web content through edge locations worldwide. It does not provide a network connection.
oa-001.d: Direct Connect links your internal network to AWS over a dedicated fiber-optic cable, bypassing the internet. However, the scenario requires using the company's existing internet connection.

oa-002.a: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that securely delivers data, videos, and APIs to global customers with low latency from multiple edge locations around the world.
oa-002.b: Amazon Translate does not automatically translate third-party website interfaces. It is a machine translation service for your own content.
oa-002.c: Deploying applications in multiple AWS Regions places resources closer to users globally, improving performance and reducing latency.
oa-002.d: Amazon Comprehend is a natural language processing (NLP) service for finding insights in text. It does not translate text or enable multi-language responses.
oa-002.e: A load balancer distributes traffic to targets within one or more Availability Zones but does not accept targets across Regions.

oa-003.a: Deploying EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones prevents a single point of failure. AZs are designed for physical redundancy and resilience.
oa-003.b: If all instances are in a single location affected by a failure, none would be available. Multiple AZs increase availability through physical redundancy.
oa-003.c: To serve cross-Region users with low latency, you need to launch instances in the second Region closer to users. Multiple AZs within one Region don't reduce cross-Region latency.
oa-003.d: Two EC2 instances in the same or different Availability Zones will not change the overall load of the application. Multiple AZs improve availability, not load.
oa-003.e: Multiple Availability Zones improve availability but do not reduce operational costs. In fact, running in multiple AZs may increase costs.

oa-004.a: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure to on-premises sites. It does not perform system migrations from on-premises to AWS.
oa-004.b: AWS SCT converts database schemas from one engine to another. It cannot migrate an entire server with its OS and database to an EC2 instance.
oa-004.c: AWS DMS migrates data between databases but does not migrate the actual server (OS + application) to an EC2 instance.
oa-004.d: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is an automated lift-and-shift solution that can migrate physical servers and any databases or applications running on them to EC2 instances.

oa-005.a: On-Demand Instances are immediately available at full price. They are not discounted and don't use unused capacity.
oa-005.b: With Spot Instances, you can access unused EC2 capacity at a significant discount — up to 90% off On-Demand prices.
oa-005.c: Reserved Instances provide a discount for committing to 1 or 3 years of usage, but this capacity is reserved for you, not unused capacity.
oa-005.d: Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to your account for compliance/licensing needs. They are not discounted unused capacity.

oa-006.a: IAM manages permissions controlling which AWS resources users can access. It does not identify security groups allowing unrestricted access.
oa-006.b: CloudTrail provides an audit record of API calls. It does not identify security groups allowing unrestricted access.
oa-006.c: Trusted Advisor checks security groups for rules allowing unrestricted access to resources, which increases risk of hacking, DoS attacks, or data loss.
oa-006.d: CloudWatch monitors and collects metrics for AWS resources. It does not identify security groups allowing unrestricted access.

oa-007.a: DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database. It provides fast performance with seamless scalability, but it is not a relational database.
oa-007.b: Amazon Aurora is a MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible relational database built for the cloud, combining enterprise performance with open source cost-effectiveness.
oa-007.c: Amazon EBS is a block-storage service for EC2 instances. While you can run a database on EC2 with EBS storage, EBS itself is not a relational database.
oa-007.d: Global Accelerator improves network performance for users' traffic by up to 60% using the AWS global network. It is not a relational database.

oa-008.a: Elastic Beanstalk deploys and scales web applications on automatically provisioned infrastructure. It does not reduce website latency for static content.
oa-008.b: Route 53 is a DNS web service for domain registration and traffic routing. With only one S3 bucket, Route 53 has only one route and cannot reduce latency.
oa-008.c: DAX reduces DynamoDB response times from milliseconds to microseconds. DynamoDB tables cannot host static websites.
oa-008.d: CloudFront is a CDN that caches static and dynamic web content at edge locations worldwide, serving content from the nearest location to reduce latency.

oa-009.a: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) creates, stores, and renews SSL/TLS certificates. You can use ACM to implement encryption in transit using protocols like TLS.
oa-009.b: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks. It cannot implement encryption of data in transit.
oa-009.c: AWS Security Hub centrally views your security posture and checks against industry standards. It cannot implement encryption of data in transit.
oa-009.d: AWS RAM shares resources across AWS accounts. It cannot implement encryption of data in transit.

oa-010.a: The reliability pillar ensures workloads perform their intended function correctly and consistently. Multi-AZ RDS deployment reduces single points of failure, supporting reliability.
oa-010.b: The security pillar protects data, systems, and assets. Multiple Availability Zones do not make an application more secure.
oa-010.c: The performance efficiency pillar focuses on using compute resources efficiently. Multiple Availability Zones do not increase performance efficiency.
oa-010.d: The cost optimization pillar focuses on delivering business value at the lowest price. Multiple Availability Zones will actually increase cost, not optimize it.

oa-011.a: The Developer Support plan allows only email creation of support tickets and does not provide phone support.
oa-011.b: The Basic Support plan provides customer support for non-technical issues like service quota increases, but does not provide technical support.
oa-011.c: The Business Support plan provides 24/7 phone, web, and chat access to Cloud Support Engineers. It is the minimum plan with phone support.
oa-011.d: The Enterprise Support plan provides phone support, but it is not the minimum plan to do so — Business is cheaper and also provides phone support.

oa-012.a: The number of versions of a Lambda function does not contribute to cost. Charges are based on requests and duration only.
oa-012.b: Lambda charges include the duration — the time it takes for your code to run, measured in milliseconds.
oa-012.c: The programming language used does not affect Lambda cost. Charges are based on requests and duration only.
oa-012.d: Lambda charges include the number of requests made for your functions.
oa-012.e: The total number of Lambda functions in an account does not affect cost. Charges are based on requests and duration only.

oa-013.a: Amazon Transcribe converts audio data to text (speech-to-text). It is not a text-to-speech service.
oa-013.b: Amazon Translate is a machine translation service for converting text between languages. It is not a text-to-speech service.
oa-013.c: Amazon Polly is a machine learning service that converts text to speech, providing the ability to read text out loud.
oa-013.d: Amazon Textract extracts text from scanned documents using OCR. It is not a text-to-speech service.

oa-014.a: Amazon SQS is a message queue for decoupling applications. It hosts queues for requests but cannot send notification alerts to a team.
oa-014.b: Amazon SNS delivers publications to subscribers via email, SMS, push notifications, etc. Ideal for alerting a team about test failures.
oa-014.c: EventBridge is a serverless event bus for connecting applications together. It is not a messaging service for delivering notification alerts to people.
oa-014.d: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service for customer engagement. It cannot send automated notification alerts.

oa-015.a: An access key ID is required for programmatic access. Together with the secret access key, it authenticates API calls to AWS.
oa-015.b: A user ID is used for IAM security credentials and console login, but not specifically for programmatic access.
oa-015.c: A secondary key is a database management concept. It does not grant AWS account access.
oa-015.d: A primary key is a database management concept. It does not grant AWS account access.
oa-015.e: A secret access key is required for programmatic access. Together with the access key ID, it authenticates API calls to AWS.

oa-016.a: Amazon Inspector is an automated security assessment for EC2 applications. It does not perform S3 data classification and discovery.
oa-016.b: Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to automatically discover and classify sensitive data in S3 buckets.
oa-016.c: GuardDuty is a threat detection service monitoring for malicious activity. It does not perform S3 data classification.
oa-016.d: Secrets Manager protects secrets like API keys and database credentials. It does not perform S3 data classification and discovery.

oa-017.a: AWS manages patching for the RDS engine as a managed service. Customers can only choose the maintenance time window.
oa-017.b: AWS controls physical access to data centers. Customers cannot visit data centers in person — only virtual tours are available.
oa-017.c: Customers are responsible for configuring IAM users with appropriate permissions following the principle of least privilege.
oa-017.d: AWS manages the operating system for Lambda as a fully managed serverless service. Customers do not patch it.
oa-017.e: Customers are responsible for configuring security groups to control inbound and outbound traffic to their EC2 instances.

oa-018.a: OpsCenter provides a central location for viewing and resolving operational work items. It does not consolidate billing or provide governance.
oa-018.b: Cost and Usage Reports consolidate billing information in a report but only for individual accounts, without cross-account billing or centralized governance.
oa-018.c: AWS Organizations provides centralized governance and consolidated billing for an AWS environment with multiple accounts.
oa-018.d: IAM Identity Center manages user access across multiple accounts but configuring it independently in each account does not provide centralized governance or consolidated billing.

oa-019.a: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center for customer service. It is not a service for connecting on-premises networks to AWS.
oa-019.b: AWS Direct Connect links your internal network to AWS through a dedicated Ethernet fiber-optic cable. It is consistent and private because your company is the only user of the cable.
oa-019.c: Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted connection using the public internet. Since the internet is a shared resource, you cannot expect consistency or true privacy.
oa-019.d: Client VPN connects individual laptops/devices to AWS, not an entire data center. It is not suitable for data center-to-cloud connectivity.

oa-020.a: Amazon S3 is an object storage service where data is stored as objects within buckets, not as files in a filesystem hierarchy.
oa-020.b: Amazon S3 provides 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability, making it one of the most durable storage systems available.
oa-020.c: Amazon S3 is not a global file system. It is an object storage service with a different access model than a file system.
oa-020.d: Amazon S3 is not a local file store. It is a cloud-based object storage service accessed over the network.
oa-020.e: Amazon S3 is not a network file system (like NFS or EFS). It is an object storage service with its own API.
